items.title: Autonomous Drug Design via Workflow Agents: Integrating Chemical Semantics and Tool-Oriented Automation
items.abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based agents have shown promise in automating scientific tasks, yet existing systems for drug discovery often lack strategic, cross-step planning, and multi-objective coordination. Here, we present drugflow-skills, an LLM-driven agent framework that abstracts key drug design operations, including virtual screening, de novo molecule generation, molecular optimization, and multi-target design, into composable and reusable skills. The agent operates under a ReAct paradigm, executing iterative “Thought → Action → Observation” loops while interfacing with the DrugFlow backend. Across five representative tasks targeting ALK, ROS1, and IGF-1R, the agent demonstrates autonomous decision-making, cross-step planning, and multi-objective trade-offs, achieving improved predicted binding scores while reducing predicted toxicity and off-target liabilities. It also provides interpretable rationales and adapts strategies based on human feedback, enabling a human-agent co-optimization loop. These results support dynamic reasoning-driven drug design.

items.title: Accelerating CO2 Biocatalysis through Multimodal AI-Guided Enzyme Prioritization and Spatial Confinement
items.abstract: Direct biological conversion of CO2 into value-added chemicals is severely restricted by sluggish enzyme kinetics and inefficient intracellular carbon flux. Here, we address these catalytic bottlenecks by synergizing multimodal deep learning, mechanistic enzyme engineering, and synthetic organelle assembly. Using CASKP, a TransKP-guided candidate-prioritization framework that integrates sequence representations with a docking-derived scalar feature, we prioritized and experimentally identified a highly active β-carbonic anhydrase, PbCA, for improving intracellular CO2 supply. Structural analysis and molecular dynamics simulations guided the design of the R71A and V112A variants. The R71A–V112A variant displayed a specific activity of 26.1 U/mg and increased the intracellular 13C-labeled 3-phosphoglycerate ratio 4.9-fold. The simulations were consistent with a more hydrated active-site environment and a strengthened Tyr108-centered hydrogen-bond network. To overcome diffusion and thermodynamic limitations, these optimized biocatalysts were encapsulated into hybrid carboxysomes and coupled with an ATP-generating carboxykinase. 13C tracing confirmed incorporation of inorganic carbon into l-malate, with 95.2% of malate detected as 13C-labeled isotopologues. Subsequent promoter optimization yielded an l-malate titer of 22.7 g/L. This multiscale approach provides an integrated strategy for heterotrophic CO2-incorporating biocatalysis.

items.title: An Antisymmetric Framework with Cross-Modal Information Decoupling for Predicting Missense Mutation-Induced Changes in Protein–Ligand Binding Affinity
items.abstract: Accurately predicting changes in protein–ligand binding affinity induced by missense mutations is important for understanding disease mechanisms, identifying drug resistance mutations, and supporting precision medicine. However, existing computational methods often directly integrate protein sequence and structure information, which may introduce background information, structural uncertainty, and redundant cross-modal information, limiting the identification of transferable mutation-related features. In addition, most existing approaches do not explicitly enforce the thermodynamic consistency of binding free energy changes upon mutation reversal. Here, we present MutBindPred, a cross-modal deep learning framework for predicting missense mutation-induced changes in protein–ligand binding affinity. MutBindPred jointly models wild-type and mutant protein–ligand complexes and introduces a cross-modal information decoupling module to separate modality-shared background information from modality-specific mutation-related signals. The framework further captures directional differences between wild-type and mutant states and incorporates an antisymmetric constraint to improve the thermodynamic consistency of predicted ΔΔG values. Under rigorous protein and ligand cold-start settings, MutBindPred achieves improved generalization performance compared with existing baseline methods. Further analyses show that sequence-derived heterogeneous representations provide the strongest transferable predictive signals. Structural representations show limited standalone predictive utility but contribute as an auxiliary modality for guiding cross-modal representation learning. Overall, MutBindPred provides a thermodynamically consistent and generalizable framework for predicting missense mutation-induced changes in protein–ligand binding affinity.

items.title: Diverse Computational Strategies Enable the Discovery of p38α−MK2 Molecular Glues
items.abstract: Mitogen-activated protein kinase-activated protein kinase 2 (MK2) phosphorylates AU-rich element-binding proteins (AUBPs) that modulate the stability of cytokine mRNA. An emerging class of inhibitors creates a ternary complex between upstream kinase p38α and MK2. These molecular glues demonstrate sustained efficacy relative to orthosteric inhibitors of either p38α or MK2; however, their mechanism of action presents challenges to computationally driven design. Herein we describe in silico hit identification strategies leveraging free energy perturbation coupled with machine learning to triage and prioritize ligands from diverse chemical sources and identify multiple structurally diverse, potent, and highly selective p38α−MK2 molecular glues. Lead compounds 14 and 28 demonstrated an attractive PK profile with sufficient coverage of human whole blood EC50 and displayed pronounced reduction of TNFα levels after PO dosing in lipopolysaccharide mouse models, illustrating the value of our in silico hit identification strategies and optimization of non-degrading molecular glues.

items.title: Organ-Selective Lipid Nanoparticles: A Landscape Review of Mechanisms, Applications, and Translational Challenges
items.abstract: Lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) are the dominant clinical platform for nucleic acid delivery, as shown by liver-directed patisiran and intramuscular mRNA-based COVID-19 vaccines. Neither involved engineered organ selectivity. Conventional four-component LNPs accumulate mainly in the liver after systemic administration, which limits their use to hepatocyte-targeted therapies. Selective organ targeting (SORT) adds a fifth, charged “SORT lipid” to the formulation. This redirects payloads to the lung, spleen, or liver in a predictable, dose-titratable manner. The leading proposed explanation is that SORT lipid alters the protein corona that forms in blood, shifting uptake away from the apolipoprotein E–low-density lipoprotein receptor pathway behind default hepatic accumulation. Consensus on this mechanism is lacking. Lipid charge and pKa, route-dependent hemodynamics, and vascular fenestration may contribute independently or in combination. We review mechanistic and translational evidence for lung-, spleen-, and liver-selective SORT formulations across three tiers: rodent, higher-order preclinical, and clinical or clinical-adjacent. We also cover bone marrow, tumor, and CNS targets and payload-specific demands. A bibliometric analysis of administration routes, corona proteins, cell types, payloads, and diseases complements this synthesis. Research volume concentrates on intravenous delivery, oncology/immunotherapy, and cystic fibrosis. Bone marrow, broader immune cell, and LSEC targeting remains comparatively underexplored. Associations between corona composition and tropism are more robust than demonstrated causality, and most direct evidence still comes from rodents, not primates or humans. We outline translational gaps and propose machine learning-guided lipid screening, combinatorial SORT–ligand targeting, and patient-specific corona profiling as priority directions for extrahepatic gene therapy, in vivo cell engineering, and precision vaccination.

items.title: De Novo Design of Catalytically Active Salen-Binding Proteins
items.abstract: De novo design of catalytic metalloproteins has the potential to generate enzymes that combine the efficiency of natural proteins with the reactivity of synthetic organometallic catalysts. Here, we develop a computational strategy to design enzymes with novel tertiary structures that bind metal salen complexes, classic small-molecule catalysts not found in biology. Six proteins were designed and screened for function; five of six express well, bind a Co-salen cofactor, and catalyze a transition metal hydrogen atom transfer (MHAT)-mediated deallylation reaction, representing the first de novo proteins to catalyze this class of transformation. The spectroscopic properties and crystal structure of the most active sequence were in excellent agreement with the design, and the holoprotein retained its structure and activity over a broad range of pH (2–12), temperatures up to 95 °C, and aqueous/organic solvent mixtures. We suggest that the combinatorial space provided by metal ion identity, ligand substitution, and active site structure can be used to generate artificial metalloenzymes that catalyze many chemical transformations.

items.title: Computational Compound Prioritization Strategy Incorporating Docking Variability and Interaction Energies Identifies Putative LRH-1 Binders
items.abstract: Compound ranking in structure-based computer-aided drug discovery notoriously yields highly ranked false positives due to sampling and, more frequently, scoring errors. We developed a compound prioritization strategy that utilizes sampled docked poses from complementary docking approaches, i.e., targeted physics-based docking and blind docking with a generative model, into multiple conformations of the target protein to train two multilayer perceptron (MLP) models. The MLPs predict binders or activators at the orthosteric ligand-binding pocket of the nuclear receptor Liver Receptor Homologue-1 (LRH-1, NR5A2). Our approach circumvents the reliance on a single docked pose for scoring compounds or individual scoring metrics for compound ranking. In an out-of-distribution compound set, we observed that the MLPs identified compounds that are chemically dissimilar from those in the training set and are sensitive to single scaffold modifications, making the MLPs potential tools for lead optimization. We applied the MLPs on a pilot study prospective drug discovery campaign, which resulted in the identification of four putative LRH-1 binders. We found that a combination of scoring and prediction metrics enriches for hit compounds across library sizes. In all, this work presents a method to leverage structural and experimental data to aid drug discovery for a challenging protein target.

items.title: From Promiscuity to Specificity: Machine Learning-Driven Multidimensional Evolution of Tropinone Reductase for Challenging Substrates
items.abstract: A fundamental challenge in harnessing substrate promiscuity for industrial biocatalysis lies in reconciling broad substrate acceptance with high catalytic specificity. Although promiscuous enzymes provide attractive starting points for accessing non-natural transformations, their native active-site architectures and conformational dynamics often lack the precision required for efficient and selective conversion of desired unnatural substrates. Thus, systematically decoding and reprogramming the interplay between promiscuity and specificity remains a key obstacle toward versatile biocatalysts. Here, we address this challenge by integrating virtual screening, machine learning, and molecular dynamics simulations into a unified engineering framework. A tropinone reductase from Cochlearia officinalis (CoTR) was identified as a broadly promiscuous scaffold. By converting complex enzyme–substrate interaction dynamics into quantifiable and actionable design principles, we predict and validate key residues that govern substrate promiscuity. Guided by these insights, distinct CoTR variants were engineered for three representative substrates. The optimized variants—CoTR‑8M, CoTR‑5M‑1, and CoTR‑5M‑2—exhibited 7.0‑ to 16.3‑fold higher catalytic efficiencies than wild-type CoTR toward their respective target substrates and supported substrate loadings of up to 50 or 100 g L–1 while maintaining >99% ee. This work not only delivers scalable routes to three industrially valuable chiral alcohols but also provides mechanistic insights into the synergistic modulation of promiscuity and specificity. This study demonstrates a general strategy for translating intricate molecular-recognition features into rational design principles, thereby facilitating the development of tailored biocatalysts for non-native substrates.

items.title: Predicting Active and Inactive Targets of Small Molecules from ChEMBL Data Using the Polypharmacology Browser PPB4
items.abstract: Drug-like molecules often interact with multiple biological targets, which must be identified during drug development. Various models spanning classical machine learning, deep learning and artificial intelligence, predict active targets of a query molecule based on its structural similarity to target annotated molecules from drug-target interaction databases such as ChEMBL. Herein we report on the Polypharmacology Browser PPB4, a deep neural network trained on ChEMBL35. In contrast to its predecessor PPB3 and related tools which only return lists of probably active targets, PPB4 also lists probably inactive targets, as well as targets that are probably both active and inactive if the query molecule is similar to both active and inactive compounds for that target. Two prospective case studies illustrate the use of PPB4, which returns every predicted target together with the list of nearest neighbor molecules marked as active on that target in the training data. PPB4 is freely available at https://ppb4.gdb.tools.

items.title: Active Learning for Fragment-Based Kinase Inhibitor Discovery using Docking
items.abstract: Drug discovery requires efficient exploration of vast chemical spaces while minimizing computational cost. Fragment-based drug design offers a promising route for generating novel ligands through recombination of fragments, yet the resulting combinatorial search spaces rapidly become too large for exhaustive evaluation. Here, we present an active learning framework for navigating kinase-focused fragment recombination spaces derived from KinFragLib. Our approach combines subpocket-aware fragment recombination, structure-based docking, machine learning surrogate models, and genetic algorithm-inspired exploration through fragment additions, deletions, and substitutions around previously evaluated ligands. Rather than screening a fully enumerated recombination library, the framework iteratively generates and evaluates promising fragment modifications, enabling scalable exploration of large recombination spaces. Using protein kinase A (PKA) as a case study, we evaluate the framework on a recombination space containing approximately 210,000 ligands. Active learning identifies high-scoring candidates while evaluating only about 0.5% of the available ligands with the computationally expensive docking workflow. A greedy acquisition strategy recovers 52% of the global top-50 ligands, substantially outperforming random sampling. In addition, a diversity-aware acquisition strategy increases fragment coverage and exploration of alternative hinge-binding motifs while retaining competitive optimization performance. These results demonstrate that active learning can efficiently navigate fragment recombination spaces and substantially reduce computational screening costs. More broadly, the proposed framework provides a transferable strategy for kinase-focused ligand design and can be extended to other targets when suitable fragment libraries are available.

items.title: Lost in Chemical Space: Local Open-Source Large Language Models Display Model-Dependent Adherence to Reference Data in Molecular Generation
items.abstract: chemical spaces remains poorly understood. Here, we evaluated Gemma-4-31B, GPT-OSS-120B, Mistral-Small-4-119B, and Qwen-3.6-35B-A3B at the BF16 (original precision), Q8, Q6, and Q4 quantization levels in two molecular generation tasks. The models were prompted either to generate small molecules without constraints or to generate drug-like molecules conditioned on 69 reference kinase inhibitors provided in-context. Quantization increased inference throughput in a modeldependent manner, with the largest gains, up to 24-fold increase in performance, occurring for Gemma-4-31B and Qwen-3.6-35B-A3B. In the task of unconstrained generation, model quantization did not affect molecular validity, uniqueness, drug-likeness, diversity and synthesizability. In the task of reference-guided generation, however, the models displayed markedly different levels of adherence to the provided chemical space. Gemma-4-31B was the only model that consistently generated small molecules similar to the reference compounds at all precision levels. Mistral-Small-4-119B and Qwen-3.6-35B-A3B failed to generate small molecules according to the reference chemical space. GPT-OSS-120B showed adherence to the reference molecules at BF16, Q8, and Q6, but lost the capacity to generate molecules in the desired chemical space at the Q4 quantization level. These results show that quantization can substantially improve the performance of local LLMs for molecular generation without compromising output quality, although model selection and validation is essential for guided exploration of the chemical space.

items.title: POLEN: An OpenMM Framework for ML/MM Simulations with Mutually Polarizable AMOEBA Embedding
items.abstract: Hybrid machine-learning and molecular mechanics formulations have been growing over the years. The attractive cost-effectiveness for big systems (such as protein complexes) has made these methods gain attention in the computational chemistry/biology field. In these theories, one of the most discussed themes is embedding, which can add or remove physics from the system. Here, we present POLEN (POLarizable Embedding for Neural-network potentials), an OpenMM plugin for ML/MM simulations with a mutually polarizable AMOEBA embedding, including a variant whose ML-trained head (MuPE(ML)) predicts multipoles, polarizabilities, and charge penetration at each simulation step. We tested it on three systems: a push-pull chromophore which a strong solvatochromic shift (p-nitroaniline in water); a protease-inhibitor complex with a buried salt bridge (trypsin-benzamidinium); and a kinase-inhibitor complex with a halogen bond (CK2α–TBB−).

items.title: Molecular function-guided unsupervised similarity-based enrichment for low-data virtual screening
items.abstract: Identifying bioactive compounds for orphan or understudied protein targets remains a significant hurdle in drug discovery due to the lack of sufficient structure-activity relationship (SAR) data. We present MolFuSE (Molecular Function-guided Similarity Explorer), an unsupervised, projection-based enrichment framework designed for low-data virtual screening and ligand repurposing. MolFuSE leverages manifold learning—specifically uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP)—to create low-dimensional similarity spaces based on a reference set of ligands known to bind proteins with the same molecular function as the target. Through systematic evaluation across nine protein targets and their functional classes, we demonstrate that UMAP embeddings of Mordred 2D descriptors act as a strong “potency filter”, significantly outperforming traditional topological fingerprints in the early enrichment of high-potency inhibitors (<100 nM). items.title: Hybrid Quantum-Classical Annealing for Protein Side-Chain Optimization: A Feasibility Study
items.abstract: Hybrid quantum-classical annealing solvers are moving from research laboratories toward industrial use, but their advantage over classical optimization appears to be confined to a narrow class of problems. A recent systematic benchmark of the D-Wave hybrid solver against industry-leading classical solvers, across several classes of optimization problems, found it to be most competitive on binary quadratic programs, while noting that few industrial problems take this form. Therefore, identifying real-world industrial problems that can be modeled with this structure is a key challenge. We propose protein side-chain optimization, a core step of computational protein design, as one of these problems: it is natively a binary quadratic program, and its application context requires pools of low-energy solutions, which annealers naturally return. In this feasibility study, we test whether the competitiveness of the hybrid solver against industry-leading classical solvers extends to this problem. On 40 instances derived from 20 experimentally determined protein structures with up to about 200 amino acids and 2000 binary variables, we compare the results achieved with a hybrid solver, run for 5 seconds, against those of the commercial solver Gurobi, run for 10 seconds, 1000 seconds, and 4 hours. items.title: On the limitations of molecular representations
items.abstract: Molecular representations such as fingerprints and learned embeddings play a central role in cheminformatics and small-molecule machine learning. They serve as the primary input for a diverse array of tasks, including clustering, dataset splitting, and virtual screening, yet their evaluation is often limited to downstream model performance on narrow benchmark tasks. We carried out a systematic investigation of the quality of molecular representations, finding that none of the state-of-the-art molecular embedding models capture graph structure, 3D shape, or ADMET endpoint similarity better than fingerprints or physicochemical descriptors. However, classical fingerprints also revealed their own material limitations. For example, we show that depending on the representation, between 225M and $\sim$4B molecules have non-unique representations in the 10.8B Enamine REAL database, with implications for virtual screening. Our findings provide an insight into the current limitations of molecular representations, outlining future research directions for the development of more robust encodings of small molecules.

items.title: A Scoping Review of Diffusion-Based De Novo Molecular Generation: Architectures, Evaluation, and Open Challenges for Computational Drug Discovery
items.abstract: Diffusion models form the bulk of generative frameworks used in de novo molecular design, yet the literature remains fragmented across model formulations, molecular representations, and generative tasks, and inadequate systematic accounts exist of how these models are steered towards molecules with desired properties, an aspect of drug discovery that is paramount to acceptance. We present a scoping review of diffusion-based neural networks applied in de novo drug discovery between 2020 and 2026. Following the PRISMA-ScR (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews) protocol, we categorise the literature into non-mutually exclusive themes covering methodological contributions, conditioning mechanisms, molecular representations, symmetries, and multi-modal integrations, and outline the datasets and evaluation metrics used throughout. Three findings emerge. First, diffusion did not displace earlier architectures so much as absorb them: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), Autoencoders, and Transformers persist as backbones, and what changed was the training objective. Second, conditioning strategies reduce to structural anchoring, target-aware biochemical conditioning, property-driven steering, and multimodal latent conditioning; within these, the point in the reverse trajectory at which a conditioning signal is applied is a design variable distinct from the signal itself. Third, evaluation remains unstandardised across frameworks, datasets, and definitions. We identify the resulting gaps in controllability and interpretability as the central open challenge for conditioned molecular generation and outline the direction to ease them as this would enable generation of molecules that match the preferred property profiles.

items.title: From Generative Molecular Design to Agentic Artificial Intelligence in Drug Discovery
items.abstract: Over the past decade, artificial intelligence (AI) has increasingly influenced the early stages of drug discovery, which focus primarily on target evaluation and the design or identification of new active small molecules or biologics. Deep neural networks adapted from areas such as natural language processing and computer vision have provided novel opportunities for generative modeling and human–machine interactions. State‐of‐the‐art AI models for generative molecular design have emerged, but remain only little understood so far. Furthermore, new computational systems are being devised rapidly that are expected to significantly transform the drug discovery landscape in the near future. These developments pose challenges to computer‐aided drug discovery in various ways. In the following, we discuss these opportunities and challenges, with a focus on molecular design.

items.title: Stimuli‐Responsive Hydrogels for Cancer Therapy: Design Strategies, Mechanisms, and Challenges in Clinical Translation
items.abstract: Stimuli‐responsive hydrogels (SRHs) are versatile soft biomaterials capable of dynamically responding to environmental cues, enabling controlled and site‐specific drug release for cancer therapy. Advances in polymer chemistry and nanotechnology have facilitated the development of SRHs that respond to tumor‐associated stimuli, including pH, redox potential, temperature, enzymatic activity, light, and glucose gradients. Among these systems, pH‐ and redox‐responsive hydrogels exploit the acidic and oxidative tumor microenvironment, while thermo‐ and photo‐responsive platforms enable spatiotemporal regulation of therapeutic payloads. Recent studies have demonstrated highly efficient, stimulus‐triggered drug release and enhanced therapeutic outcomes in vitro and in vivo. This review systematically examines the design strategies, molecular mechanisms, and structure–function relationships governing SRHs in oncology. Emerging hydrogel architectures—such as injectable systems, hybrid nanocomposites, and multifunctional platforms integrating targeting or imaging capabilities—are critically discussed. Importantly, the review addresses key challenges in clinical translation, including biocompatibility, scalability, regulatory considerations, and reproducibility. Finally, future perspectives are outlined, highlighting the potential of artificial intelligence‐assisted material design, computational modeling, and wearable or implantable bioelectronic interfaces for real‐time monitoring and adaptive cancer therapy. By integrating mechanistic insights with translational and regulatory viewpoints, this review aims to guide the rational development of next‐generation smart hydrogel therapeutics for clinical oncology.

items.title: The Limited Contribution of Structural Information Relative to Language-Model Signal in Data-Limited Cryptic Pocket Prediction
items.abstract: Cryptic pockets, drug-binding sites absent from a protein’s static structure but exposed through conformational change, expand the scope of druggable targets, yet remain difficult to identify computationally. PocketMiner, a structure-based graph neural network trained on molecular dynamics simulation data, predicts cryptic pocket formation from a single static structure (ROC-AUC 0.87). Recent protein language model (PLM)-based approaches report further improvements over this structure-only baseline (up to 0.93), but do so by simultaneously replacing the structural architecture with a sequence-only model and switching to substantially larger, differently-sourced training data–leaving it unclear whether these gains stem from the languagemodel signal itself or from increased training data scale. We isolate this variable directly: holding architecture family and PocketMiner’s original, small molecular-dynamics-derived training set fixed, we compare three matched variants–geometry-only (baseline), ESM2 embeddings only, and both combined (fused)–under identical training conditions. The geometry-only baseline achieves chance-level test performance (ROC-AUC 0.498), while both the ESM2-only (0.817) and fused (0.835) variants perform far above it, with statistically indistinguishable confidence intervals between the two, indicating that language-model signal alone accounts for nearly all of the achievable performance, and that structural information contributes marginally under these conditions. This result is confirmed on CryptoBench, an independent, larger benchmark (baseline 0.494 vs. fused 0.716, non-overlapping confidence intervals), and holds consistently across every pocket-formation mechanism examined in a stratified analysis. These findings suggest that a substantial share of the improvement reported by prior sequence-based methods is attributable to language-model signal itself rather than training data scale, with implications for data-efficient strategies in structure-based pocket prediction more broadly.

items.title: PABbind: A Hierarchical Geometric Framework for Mutation-Involved Antigen−Antibody Interaction Prediction and SARS-CoV-2 Immune Escape Assessment
items.abstract: Antibody therapies exhibit remarkable specificity and therapeutic potential, yet their efficacy can be compromised by rapidly emerging antigen mutations that enable immune escape. Therefore, predicting how antigen variants alter antibody recognition is critical for assessing antibody durability, but experimental evaluation of large-scale mutation combinations remains challenging. Here, we develop PABbind, a hierarchical geometric deep-learning model that integrates sequence and structural information to predict antigen−antibody interaction changes using wild-type protein−protein interaction (PPI) structures and mutant sequences. By simultaneously incorporating sequence and structural information and leveraging pretraining on general mutant PPI datasets, PABbind accurately predicts immune escape effects of antigen variants against antibodies using wild-type PPI structures only, enabling large-scale screening of antigen mutations. PABbind demonstrates favorable performance on mutant PPI benchmarks and enables prediction of variant-specific immune escape scores for SARS-CoV-2 antibodies, therefore providing an effective computational framework for large-scale assessment of SARS-CoV-2 antigen variants.

items.title: DEL-Flow: AI-Driven Structural Generation and Activity Validation of MDM2-Targeting Macrocyclic Peptides
items.abstract: Macrocyclic peptides represent a promising modality for modulating intracellular protein–protein interactions; however, macrocyclic peptide datasets with reliable experimental activity measurements that can inform rational design remain limited. Here, we developed DEL-Flow, a pocket-conditioned generative framework for the design of MDM2-p53 inhibitors. Using an iterative DEL-selection strategy, a first-generation symmetric dimeric macrocyclic peptide DEL identified a half-scaffold associated with highly enriched library members, which was retained to construct a second-generation asymmetric focused DEL. Experimentally derived selection signals from this focused DEL were combined with computationally generated conformations and macrocyclic topologies for model training. DEL-Flow integrates these priors with MDM2 pocket and PackDock-derived pose information to generate side-chain variants while retaining the macrocyclic core. An SE(3)-equivariant flow-matching model generates all-atom coordinates, and a MASK denoising module predicts editable-region atom types, chirality, and bond connectivity. Starting from templates 126 and 319, DEL-Flow generated 20 candidates from each template, yielding 40 candidates in total. Following prioritization, 126-18 and 319-18 were synthesized off DNA and inhibited the MDM2-p53 interaction in fluorescence-polarization assays, with IC50 values of 1.95 and 6.50 μM and Ki values of 163 and 548 nM, respectively. These results support the use of DEL selection signals and pocket geometry to guide the generation of macrocyclic peptides absent from the original library that inhibit the MDM2–p53 interaction.

items.title: A Machine Learning Approach to logBB Prediction Combining Molecular Docking and Quantum-Chemical Descriptors
items.abstract: Blood–brain barrier (BBB) permeability is a major challenge in the development of drugs targeting the central nervous system (CNS). Computational prediction methods can help prioritize candidate compounds and reduce the experimental workload during early drug discovery. In this study, machine learning models were developed to predict the blood-to-brain concentration ratio expressed as its decimal logarithm (logBB). The objective was to investigate whether molecular docking scores obtained with AutoDock Vina for P-glycoprotein (P-gp) and breast cancer resistance protein (BCRP), together with quantum-chemical descriptors, could provide additional information for logBB prediction. The dataset comprised 685 compounds. A linear regression analysis identified eight factors associated with logBB: hydrogen bond donors, gas-phase electronic energy, electronic energy difference between water and hexane, number of heavy atoms, LogP, gas-phase geometry optimization time, number of aromatic rings, and fraction of sp3-hybridized carbon atoms. Notably, the electronic energy difference between water and hexane showed a stronger association with logBB than the corresponding Gibbs free energy difference, suggesting that electronic energy descriptors may provide complementary information. Higher-level quantum-chemical calculations will be required to investigate this finding further. Twenty-one machine learning models were evaluated. The selected support vector regression model using a radial basis function kernel (SVR-RBF; C = 0.869, ε = 0.135, γ = 0.165) was trained on 585 compounds and evaluated on a held-out validation set of 100 compounds, achieving an R2 of 0.605, an MAE of 0.368, and an RMSE of 0.459. Finally, the computational time analysis showed that descriptor generation was strongly dependent on molecular weight, with quantum-chemical calculations and molecular docking accounting for most of the computational cost. Overall, this work highlights the potential of combining physicochemical, molecular docking, and quantum-chemical descriptors for machine learning-based logBB prediction.

items.title: HyperDFI: Cross-View Hypergraph-Graph Contrastive Learning for Drug-Food Interaction Prediction
items.abstract: Drug-food interactions (DFIs) are one of the major factors that trigger adverse drug events and have important research and clinical application value. However, experimental identification of DFIs remains costly and limited in scalability, leading to insufficient coverage of known interactions. Existing computational methods often treat DFI prediction as a variant of drug-drug interaction (DDI) prediction and primarily focus on drug-food constituent relationships, which restrict their ability to directly model drug-food interactions. In this study, we propose a cross-view hypergraph-graph contrastive learning framework named HyperDFI for predicting interactions between drug and food (food constituents). We first construct four benchmark data sets by integrating information from DrugBank and PubMed, covering both drug-food and drug-food constituent interactions. Based on these data sets, heterogeneous bipartite graphs were established. HyperDFI jointly captures local topological structures and global high-order semantic relationships by combining graph neural networks (GNNs) and dynamic hypergraph neural networks (HGNNs). Furthermore, a cross-view contrastive learning strategy is introduced to align representations at different structural scales, thereby enhancing their consistency and discriminability. Extensive experiments on four benchmark data sets demonstrate that HyperDFI consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods. In addition, case studies on grapefruit further validate its ability to uncover novel DFIs.

items.title: A Latent Ability Model for Benchmarking Molecular Representations
items.abstract: The growing number of chemical foundation models calls for a standardized benchmarking method both for practitioners choosing representations and researchers identifying gaps. Previous work that ranked latent abilities of various chemical embeddings to predict ADMET properties suffered from significant shortcomings, including the use of biased datasets incongruent with real world usage and overstating statistically significant differences in model performance. We derive from first principles a variance inflation factor of (M+1)/3 for the Bayesian Bradley-Terry model evaluating M models on E endpoints at the exchangeable null and use numerical simulation to show variance inflation is still present in the non-exchangeable case. We propose a new method to directly model the margin of error as a function of latent ability and use it to evaluate models retrospectively on the datasets from the OpenADMET Polaris, ExpansionRx, and PXR competitions. We compare 35 embeddings and 13 end-to-end fine-tuned models across 17 ADMET endpoints. Although endpoint-to-endpoint variability means that no neural representation is expected to outperform ECFP on a hypothetical new endpoint in more than 95% of cases, our model concludes that 29 of 47 representations outperform ECFP in terms of latent ability with posterior probability above 0.95.

items.title: Closed-loop formulation–process optimization under unknown feasibility for extended-release pellets
items.abstract: Pharmaceutical formulation development frequently encounters formulation–process conditions that fail before a viable product is produced, leaving downstream performance unobservable and experimental feasibility unknown a priori. Here, we demonstrate a closed-loop formulation-development workflow that jointly optimizes formulation and process variables while learning experimental feasibility from physical outcomes. Using caffeine-loaded extended-release pellets produced by wet granulation and extrusion-spheronization, ANDROMEDA 1 selected formulation compositions and processing conditions within a large mixed categorical and numerical design space. Across 51 experiments performed in 13 sequential batches, 29 conditions produced pellets suitable for downstream characterization and 22 (43%) were infeasible. Failed experiments were retained as feasibility observations without assigning artificial drug release scores. Among feasible formulations, the best observed deviation from a predefined four-hour zero-order release target decreased from 1.63 to 0.17 fraction-hours. Release performance, pellet morphology and drug loading followed distinct trajectories, with an empirical trade-off between release deviation and median pellet aspect ratio. Retrospective Gaussian-process modelling showed that replacing an excipient-slot encoding with slot-independent material mass fractions increased leave-one-out cross validated R2 for release prediction from 0.39 to 0.60. Adding four derived wet-mass descriptors reduced release prediction R2 to 0.38 but yielded the highest morphology prediction R2 (0.64). Neither alternative representation improved forward-in-time release prediction. Together, these results show that unknown feasibility, competing product attributes and formulation representation can be incorporated within a single adaptive formulation-process workflow. Analyses further identify design space coverage and representation choice as important considerations for machine learning-guided pharmaceutical development.

items.title: Molecular Prior Networks
items.abstract: Predicting affinity between small molecules and their protein targets remains one of the central problems in drug discovery. Due to the substantial cost of wet-lab experiments, machine learning models of drug-target affinity are usually trained on relatively small datasets, ranging from tens to hundreds of molecules. Given the inherent difficulty of generalization between different targets and chemical series, existing datasets of protein-ligand affinities are typically not used for new projects. At the same time, tabular foundation models, including Prior-data Fitted Networks, have recently shown how transformers can be used to solve machine learning problems in a single forward pass of the network, after being trained over a large corpus of, typically, synthetic datasets. Inspired by that line of work, we propose a novel affinity modelling approach, in which the labels of the query molecules are predicted from the labelled support molecules in a single forward pass of a transformer model. The model is trained on thousands of existing affinity datasets, enabling it to capture the general patterns of molecular activity across different targets, chemical series and dataset sizes. For the smallest support sets, our model matches the state of the art on the regression variant of the FS-Mol benchmark, while being faster than existing methods, thanks to the lack of task-specific training. A comparison against a reduced variant of our architecture, which amounts to kernel regressio

items.title: Evaluating the Dimensionality of Molecular Ensembles Using Deep Neural Network Stochastic Autoencoders
items.abstract: Stochastic autoencoders (SAEs), which omit the Kullback–Leibler prior-matching term of variational autoencoders and are therefore suited to reconstruction rather than generative sampling, offer a nonlinear route to reducing the dimensionality of molecular ensembles, but their behavior across systems of differing size and flexibility is poorly characterized. Training SAEs on molecular dynamics trajectories of oxycodone, deca-alanine, crambin, a bromodomain–JQ1 complex, and HIV-1 protease, we find that reconstruction error plateaus at a system- and model-dependent latent dimensionality, that the effects of dropout and batch normalization are system-specific, and that SAEs yield more distinct clusters than principal component analysis (PCA) at very low dimensionality and reconstruct large data sets more accurately than the deterministic autoencoder CompressTraj at low dimensionality. With two to four latent variables, SAE reconstructions of crambin and HIV-1 protease are as accurate as PCA with 6–18 components, two latent variables span their leading principal subspace as well as 9–15 components, and a single SAE coordinate recovers the end-to-end distance of deca-alanine (R2 = 0.97, versus 0.04 for the first principal component), whereas PCA is more accurate at higher dimensionality and for the near-rigid bromodomain ensemble. Latent-space perturbations show that SAE latent variables encode nonlinear, position-dependent collective motions that vary across the learned manifold.

items.title: From Artificial Intelligence Outputs to Medicinal Chemistry Decisions in Kinase Inhibitor Discovery: Evidence Boundaries, Resistance-Aware Design, and DMTA Learning
items.abstract: Kinase inhibitor discovery increasingly requires integrated decision-making that extends beyond biochemical potency. Selecting the next analogue, defining the assay package, evaluating structural hypotheses, anticipating resistance, and assessing developability collectively require evidence from distinct experimental layers. In this Perspective, we argue that the practical value of artificial intelligence-assisted drug discovery (AIDD) in kinase inhibitor programs should be assessed not by predictive performance alone but by whether computational outputs improve medicinal chemistry decisions that can be implemented and experimentally tested. We treat AI-supported outputs as testable hypotheses whose value is determined by their effect on analogue selection, assay prioritization, resistance panel design, and information gain across Design−Make−Test−Analyze (DMTA) cycles. Using resistance-focused examples from EGFR, ALK/ROS1/TRK, BCR−ABL1, and BTK, we illustrate how explicit evidence boundaries, validation gates, and falsifying experiments can guide redesign decisions and learning updates.

items.title: End-to-End Prediction of Subcutaneous Peptide Absorption Rates from Amino Acid Sequences Using Physics-Informed Machine Learning
items.abstract: The subcutaneous (SC) absorption rate constant (ka) dictates critical pharmacokinetic and dosing parameters of injectable peptide therapeutics, yet currently, it cannot be predicted prior to clinical testing, forcing empirical decisions at the discovery and formulation stages. We address this important gap by constructing the first end-to-end machine learning framework that predicts SC ka, both point predictions and prediction intervals, purely from the amino acid sequence and conjugate chemistry. For developing the model, we first curated a comprehensive database of 41 human clinical ka values (0.0077−7.61 h−1), covering unmodified, fatty-acid-acylated, and protein-conjugated peptides. These data were subsequently encoded into a combination of protein language model (ESM-2) embeddings, chemical language model (ChemBERTa) embeddings, and 30 physics-informed molecular descriptors designed to capture the physical variables governing SC transport. Seven machine learning (ML) architectures and ensembles thereof were trained, with the best model (NGBoost) achieving R2 = 0.850 under leave-one-out cross-validation, a markedly high accuracy given the large variance in the clinically reported ka values. Notably, models trained on the physics-informed molecular descriptors or combinations thereof substantially outperformed models trained purely on learned embeddings (ESM-2, ChemBERTa)a direct consequence of the small scale of our training dataset. SHAP interpretability analysis indicates that predictions are consistent with established SC absorption physics, with properties including molecular weight, net charge, hydrophobicity, and acyl chain molecular characteristics dictating model predictions. Leveraging Jackknife+, the developed framework also reports ka prediction uncertainties (prediction intervals). Overall, this framework enables high-throughput sequence-level candidate ranking before in vivo data become available, supporting the rational early-stage development of peptide therapeutics.

items.title: Identifying Short Half-Life Compounds from Structure Information Using Multi-Task Graph Neural Networks
items.abstract: Accurate prediction of terminal half-life (t1/2) is paramount for prioritizing drug candidates during the lead optimization stage, as it minimizes the risk of clinical trial failure while optimizing resource allocation. Drugs characterized by suboptimal t1/2 profileseither excessively short or prolongedpresent significant challenges in dosage design and are frequently associated with increased risks of adverse effects. Traditionally, the determination of t1/2 has necessitated in vivo experiments to derive total clearance (CLT) and volume of distribution (Vss). In this study, we curated a comprehensive dataset of over 1400 compounds and developed deep learning-based regression models to predict t1/2 directly from molecular structures using Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs). We implemented both single-task and multi-task learning architectures; the latter integrated CLT, Vss, and other related pharmacokinetic parameters to leverage their inherent physiological correlations. Our results indicate that a multi-task model achieved higher predictive performance than the single-task counterpart, with notably high precision in identifying compounds with short t1/2. By enabling the structural-based identification of unfavorable t1/2 profiles without the need for experimental data, this approach provides a robust and efficient tool for streamlining candidate selection in the early stages of drug development. This methodology is expected to accelerate the discovery of compounds with favorable pharmacokinetic properties, reducing the reliance on late-stage experimental validation.

items.title: Auditing frozen chemical language model embeddings for drug-delivery screening: fingerprint baselines, random-initialization controls, and scaffold-memorization control tasks
items.abstract: Frozen embeddings from pretrained chemical language models (cLMs) are widely used as features for ADMET and drug-delivery prediction, often with a linear probe and little validation of what the representation actually contributes. We audit two small public cLMs (ChemBERTa-77M-MLM and ChemBERTa-77M-MTR, 3.4M parameters each) on three delivery-relevant endpoints from openly licensed sources: blood–brain barrier penetration (B3DB, CC0), PAMPA permeability (NCATS via PubChem), and Caco-2 permeability (OpenADMET, CC-BY-4.0). For each endpoint we compare frozen mean-pooled embeddings with (i) Morgan-fingerprint linear probes with train-only tuned regularization, (ii) the same architecture with random weights (five initialization seeds), and (iii) scaffoldconstant control tasks in the style of Hewitt and Liang that quantify how much a linear probe can score by memorizing scaffold identity. On observed means, tuned fingerprint probes are slightly ahead of frozen embeddings on all three endpoints (paired per-split differences of 0.016–0.032 in AUROC or R2, smaller than split-to-split variation); trained embeddings exceed random-initialization controls by 0.04–0.10; endpoint probes are selective above scaffold-memorization controls, and the memorization ceiling rises with layer depth in the primary MLM model. Decodability of bulk physicochemical descriptors (molecular weight, TPSA, fraction sp3, aromatic rings) is largely preserved under random initialization, indicating an architectural rather than learned origin for those signals; learned increments appear for logP, hydrogen-bond donors, and rotatable bonds. We quantify three practitioner pitfalls: pooling choice changes endpoint AUROC by up to 0.05; tuning the fin- gerprint baseline’s regularization changes it by up to 0.03 AUROC or 0.20 R2; and scaffoldsplit construction details change means by up to 0.04, exceeding seed standard deviations. The source datasets are public and cited; all curation scripts, pipeline code, and per-seed results are included in the accompanying package. The study is compute-bounded to CPU and small models, which limits the generality of the conclusions to that regime.

items.title: Integrating artificial intelligence and molecular simulation for peptide discovery: limitations, validation and decision-centered workflows
items.abstract: Summary. Therapeutic peptides occupy a chemical and pharmacological space between smallmolecules and biologics, offering extended recognition surfaces and access to targets that resist conventionalmodalities. Their discovery, however, requires the simultaneous optimization of activity, selectivity, stability, permeability and synthetic feasibility across a conformationally complex and chemically heterogeneous search space. Artificial intelligence (AI) andmolecular simulation address complementary aspects of this problem: AI learns structure–property relationships and explores large candidate libraries, whereas simulation interrogates conformational ensembles, target recognition and membrane-associated behaviour within an explicit physical model. We organize the field around a single, more discriminating question: under which chemical, biological and decision-making conditions does adding molecular simulation to an AI workflow improve peptide discovery outcomes enough to justify its cost? To answer it, we introduce a decision framework linking peptide chemistry and discovery endpoint to the decision beingmade, the uncertainty limiting that decision, the evidence that computation or experiment can provide, the cost of obtaining that evidence and the criterion for proceeding or stopping. Recent advances in biomolecular structure prediction, protein language models, generative design andmacrocycle engineering supply powerful enabling capabilities, but their transfer to short, flexible, cyclic and chemically modified peptides remains unevenly validated. Critically, a structured survey of 15 integrated studies shows that none (0 of 15) included a matched-budget comparison against an AI-only or conventional baseline, a scarcity we treat as a central empirical finding rather than an inconvenience. We outline reporting, benchmarking and prospective-validation standards by which genuine progress should be judged, and define what ‘developable’ must mean at the hit, lead and candidate stages.

items.title: Design and Benchmarking of CK2α′-Preferring Inhibitors for Huntington’s Disease: The Limits of Structure-Based Isoform Selectivity
items.abstract: Protein kinase CK2 acts through two catalytic isoforms, CK2α (A1) and CK2α′ (A2), whose ATP-binding sites differ at only two hinge positions, making isoform-selective inhibition difficult. We tested whether a standard structure-based pipeline can design and rank CK2α′-preferring compounds. In a paired benchmark of 140 compounds measured against both isoforms, none of the five docking-derived criteria, computed with GNINA and convolutional neural network rescoring, correlated with measured selectivity (ρ = −0.19 to +0.12), and for matched pairs differing by a single linker methylene, the scoring reversed the experimental order. The only reliable determinant of preference, a two-carbon linker within the benzo[c][2,6]naphthyridine scaffold, was obtained from the measured activities rather than from any computed score. Molecular-dynamics ensembles of the two isoforms overlapped (0.88 Å between versus 0.72–0.96 Å within), placing the selectivity signal below the resolution of the methods. From an enumerated series, EV043 showed the largest end-point free-energy preference for CK2α′ (ΔΔGb -7.74 kcal/mol), although this value remained sensitive to the starting pose in CK2α, while the non-selective inhibitor CX-4945 was reproduced correctly (+0.08 kcal/mol). Distinguishing CK2α′ from CK2α therefore requires alchemical free-energy methods supported by experimental validation.

items.title: Benchmarking Machine Learning Models for Viral Nanobody Epitope Prediction
items.abstract: Rapid development of therapeutics against emerging viral pathogens increasingly depends on machine learning (ML), both to generate candidate binders and for structural validation. Nanobodies (Nbs), or single-domain antibodies, are promising antiviral therapeutics, but accurate in silico prediction of viral epitopes remains challenging. Here we benchmark three ML-based structure prediction models, Boltz-2, Chai-1 and AlphaFold3 (AF3), against a curated data set of viral antigen-nanobody complexes deposited after the AF3 training cutoff. AF3 outperformed the other models: success (interface DockQ > 0.23) rose from 33% with a single seed to 50% and 65% with 10 and 100 seeds-per-target, respectively, compared with 18% for Boltz-2 and 30% for Chai-1. Using an expanded data set, we evaluated confidence metrics and found that a strict ipTM cutoff of 0.8, or a combination of ipTM ≥ 0.6 with a CDR3 loop pLDDT ≥ 60, reliably excluded incorrect predictions while retaining most successful ones. We further establish best practices for two AF3-specific capabilities, the choice of antigen multimeric state and the inclusion of N-glycosylation, both of which can be decisive for epitope success depending on the target. Finally, we apply these guidelines to two design problems: ranking a library of VEEV-neutralizing nanobodies and mapping the epitope of the broadly neutralizing nanobody CC3 across homologous alphavirus antigens. These results provide a practical framework for ML-based viral nanobody epitope prediction and design.

items.title: ProteoCraft: Protein Design as Proposal-Verification Search
items.abstract: Protein-protein interactions underpin nearly all biological processes. Yet, designing proteins with desired interactions remains challenging due to the structural complexity governing molecular recognition. This study views protein design as a search optimization problem over a combinatorial sequence space under expensive structural evaluation. Toward this goal, we introduce a novel tree-based search framework, ProteoCraft, that employs approximate structural gradients from diffusion-based structure predictors as effective proposal policies to specify where the search should explore. Complete no-gradient inference of folding models separately assigns values to the resulting sequences, determining what is good. ProteoCraft allocates this verification budget through a coarse-to-fine paradigm: multi-site edits first explore distinct sequence basins, then verified promising states undergo strict single-site refinement. Across fourteen de novo binder-design settings spanning eight target proteins, five immune-relevant TCR-facing targets, and four localized CDR redesign tasks, ProteoCraft improves design quality and high-confidence yield. These improvements persist under independent AF2-IG and Rosetta-based interface evaluation. Prospective experimental validation further yielded an 82.9% binding hit rate for PD-L1 miniproteins, with a best measured KD of 0.879 nM, and confirmed binding of designed IFNAR2 VHH. Our code is available at https://github.com/smiles724/ProteoCraft_v1.

items.title: El Agente Fármaco: A Scalable AI Scientist for Drug Discovery
items.abstract: Computational drug discovery offers a growing range of tools for proposing and evaluating molecules, but combining them and deciding what to do next still requires substantial expert effort. Here, we introduce El Agente Fármaco, an AI scientist that uses modern large language model (LLM) technology to turn discovery goals expressed in everyday language into complex, scalable computational screening workflows. The agentic harness selects scientific tools, reviews their results, and adjusts subsequent steps to the target and the user's objectives. Our approach centers on a shared scientific memory: Fármaco Atlas, which stores molecules, structures, and results together with their provenance -- a record of how they were obtained. The agent uses targeted database queries to retrieve the evidence needed for each decision. A single request can launch calculations for an entire collection of molecules, without requiring a separate LLM decision for every compound. This design limits the information the model must process as screening collections grow, while keeping the underlying results available for inspection and further analysis. The integrated tools support molecule generation, prediction of binding and molecular properties, and searches for compounds available for purchase. In a retrospective comparison with an expert-led campaign, the agent proposed chemically distinct candidates with competitive docking scores and higher calculated drug-likeness under explicitly imposed selec

items.title: RangeFinder: Predicting Ligand Property Ranges from Protein Pockets
items.abstract: Identifying ligands for a protein target requires searching a vast chemical space for a comparatively small set of compatible molecules. Existing machine learning approaches primarily address this problem by generating candidate ligands or scoring individual protein-ligand pairs, but provide limited information about the broader chemical space compatible with a binding pocket. We introduce RangeFinder, an SE(3)-equivariant transformer pocket-level model, trained and evaluated on BioLiP2 data, that predicts ranges over nine physicochemical ligand properties directly from pocket structure, chemistry, and evolutionary context. Using an intersection-over-union objective and evaluation metric (range-IoU), RangeFinder achieves a range-IoU of $0.464 \pm 0.002$, outperforming all deployable baselines while requiring only $12.2$ ms per pocket. We also quantify our method's ability to reduce the ligand search space while retaining compatible binders; in this regard, RangeFinder achieves a Reduction-Recall F-Score of $0.543 \pm 0.011$ --- once again outperforming all deployable baselines. Ablation experiments indicate that RangeFinder's performance depends more strongly on the density and quality of ligand supervision than on any individual input modality or specialized training strategy. Together, these results position RangeFinder as an inexpensive and effective molecular filtering prior, with demonstrated potential in narrowing the ligand search space of target pockets before docking

items.title: ADMET property prediction and toxicity profiling of CDK2 inhibitors: a practical cheminformatics tutorial using ADMET-AI 2.0 and RDKit
Can agents reliably design therapeutic antibodies?
items.abstract: Recent work has demonstrated agents driving protein design workflows, either through orchestration of specialized tools or direct manipulation of sequences. Yet the fidelity with which agents follow protein design instructions and the factors contributing to their effectiveness remain understudied. We examine agentic antibody design under two settings: when explicit molecular-editing instructions are provided and when agents receive only previously-scored sequences and are prompted to propose improvements. We call the first task-guided and the second black-box design. For the task-guided setting, we curate ten expert-validated affinity-improvement tasks and show that LLM judges closely reproduce programmatic evaluations of instruction following. We then study two augmentations: access to antibody-relevant tools and to previously scored design history. Tools improve instruction following (IF) and sequence space exploration while reducing optimization performance, whereas design history reduces IF but improves optimization performance at the expense of exploration. Finally, we combine taskguided and black-box design within an in silico optimization loop and show that our agentic optimizer performs comparably to an established Bayesian optimization baseline.

items.title: What Are LLM Agents Actually Learning on Low-Budget Molecular Optimization Benchmarks?
items.abstract: Recent work reports large gains for LLM agents on low-budget molecular optimization. We measure the contributions of online optimization, retrievable task information, and permissive oracle landscapes. On PMO at 50 oracle calls, a GPT-4o mini agent's sum AUC falls from 14.44 to 4.85 after task names and curated reference compounds are hidden. An identity-blinded condition that states only the oracle form (e.g., similarity to a hidden reference) scores 5.39, while a deterministic retrieval-only baseline with no LLM reaches 12.16 (84% of the full agent). A full 23-task 2x2 ablation and a three-seed replication on eight tasks support this interpretation. On a protein-targeted benchmark with an AutoDock Vina composite oracle, a single-edit random walk is a strong lower bound; across three seeds it obtains composite 0.636 +/- 0.008 and docking improvement -1.11 +/- 0.04 kcal/mol. As a positive control, a retrieval-free population agent exceeds REINVENT at a matched 50-call AUC budget, with its strongest result at 100 calls. These results motivate two inexpensive sanity checks: retrieval-safe PMO prompts and a random-walk floor for docking-based optimization.

items.title: Sequence Scanning Improves Accuracy for Antibody–Antigen and Molecular Glue Ternary Complex Cofolding
items.abstract: Accurately modeling biomolecular interactions is crucial for understanding biological function and can accelerate drug discovery efforts. Deep‐learning‐based cofolding methods such as AlphaFold3 and Boltz‐2 can successfully predict many different biomolecular complexes. However, these models show lower success rates in predicting antibody–antigen and molecular glue (MG) ternary complexes, two cases of high relevance to pharmaceutical research. Here, we present sequence scanning, a new workflow, evaluated on Boltz and Protenix, that improves prediction accuracy in these domains by applying systematic constraints to enhance overall sampling diversity. For both use cases, we assess the performance of the method on large, diverse benchmark sets. We find improved accuracy of the sequence scanning workflow in predicting antibody–antigen interface contacts and in pose prediction quality for MGs compared to previously published results. We also discuss remaining challenges and potential improvements to the method.

items.title: DELBERT-2: Pretrained Fingerprint Language Models for DEL Protein Binder Prediction
items.abstract: We present DELBERT-2, a pretrained fingerprint language model that converts sparse molecular fingerprints into unified token sequences using a ModernBERT encoder trained with masked language modelling on 2.5M molecules from the AIRCHECK DEL corpus. We evaluate across six targets (WDR91, WDR12, SETDB1, PLCZ1, LRRK2, DCAF7) under three out-of-distribution (OOD) protocols: hierarchical cluster splits probe chemical novelty, library splits test cross-library transfer, and building-block splits assess compositional generalization. DELBERT-2 consistently improves PR-AUC and NDCG@1000 relative to LightGBM ensemble baselines and transformers trained from scratch, with the largest gains in stringent OOD regimes. DELBERT-2 achieves 13.28+/-3.72 enrichment factor at top-100 vs. 12.36+/-3.75 for no-pretraining (p=0.040), representing 7.4% improvement and 13x enrichment over random selection. These results demonstrate that fingerprint-centric self-supervised learning effectively improves hit prioritization under distribution shift, enabling practical DEL virtual screening. Code is available at \hyperlink{https://github.com/GenerativeDrugDiscovery/DELBERT-2}{DELBERT-2}.

items.title: Transferring Peptide-Target Interaction Patterns to Small Molecules by Joint Guidance for Diffusion and Flow Matching
items.abstract: Generating small molecules to target protein-protein interactions (PPIs) remains one of the most challenging yet high-reward frontiers in drug discovery. Unlike traditional small-molecule drugs that bind to deep, well-defined pockets, PPI interfaces often comprise broad, shallow binding surfaces. A natural strategy is to leverage known peptide-target interactions, as peptide ligands provide rich interface-level constraints. However, a major algorithmic challenge is that rigid atom-level conditioning on peptide structures can over-constrain the generative space and exclude valid small-molecule solutions. To address this challenge, we present PIFT (Peptide InterFace Transfer), a novel framework that transfers peptide-target interaction patterns to small molecules through joint sampling-time guidance of masked discrete diffusion and continuous flow matching. PIFT first maps peptide-target and small-molecule-target interfaces into a shared, target-conditioned interaction space, capturing transferable interface information across molecular modalities. The resulting peptide-derived reference then jointly steers building-block logits and 3D coordinates toward peptide-compatible molecules while preserving a strong adapted molecular prior. Extensive experiments across diverse PPI targets show that the learned representation captures cross-modal interaction compatibility, while peptide guidance improves interface recovery and achieves strong docking performance and favorable molecular

items.title: THP-NanoTarget: leakage-aware cheminformatics for tumor-homing peptide evaluation and conservative analog prioritization
items.abstract: Public tumor-homing peptide (THP) resources have enabled predictors such as THPep, SCMTHP, StackTHPred, StackTHP and LLM4THP. At the same time, broader peptide machine-learning resources, including the recent PepBenchmark/PepBenchData initiative, are moving the field toward standardized datasets, preprocessing, and leaderboards across peptide-property tasks. These developments have improved comparability but have not removed task-specific problems in THP modelling: available THP benchmarks are motif-rich, chemically redundant, and susceptible to optimistic evaluation under near-neighbor overlap and potential leakage. A cheminformatics evaluation of THP predictions therefore needs to ask not only whether a peptide receives a high score, but also whether that score is independent, motif-driven, chemically redundant, hard-negative-sensitive, or near-duplicate-dependent. We present THP-NanoTarget, a reproducible peptide-cheminformatics framework for leakage-aware THP benchmarking, motif-rule comparisons, Morgan/ECFP chemical-space auditing, hard-negative evaluations, strict external-recognition filtering, and conservative analog prioritization. The primary benchmark contained 4202 peptides: 1401 THP positives and 2801 primary negatives. items.title: TACFormer: Transformer-Based Generative Model for Target-Conditioned De Novo PROTAC Design
items.abstract: Targeted protein degradation (TPD) represents a fundamental shift in drug discovery, moving beyond traditional target inhibition toward the event-driven removal of disease-causing proteins. A prominent strategy for TPD is the use of proteolysis-targeting chimeras (PROTACs), heterobifunctional molecules that selectively route a protein of interest (POI) to the ubiquitin-proteasome system for degradation. While PROTAC design still relies heavily on trial-and-error synthesis and experimental testing, deep generative models offer a promising means to explore PROTAC chemical space in silico and generate novel molecules. However, many existing generative methods formulate PROTAC design primarily as a linker-generation problem, with POI-binding (warhead) and E3-ligase-binding components fixed in advance. This restricts exploration of the full PROTAC chemical space and often leaves the POI implicit through the predefined warhead, rather than using protein-level information as an explicit conditioning signal during generation. To address these limitations, we propose TACFormer: a transformer-based generative model for target-aware de novo PROTAC design. The model conditions a GPT-style molecular decoder on pretrained ESM-2 representations of POI sequences, allowing POI-level information to steer full-molecule generation. items.title: What to randomize matters: a controlled study of volume, axis and representation in low-data molecular generation
items.abstract: Chemical language models can struggle to generate new molecules when trained on small datasets, where a model may reproduce training examples rather than learn a useful generative distribution. Randomized SMILES augmentation varies atom traversal, whereas Sequential Attachment-based Fragment Embedding (SAFE) also allows the order of fragment blocks to vary. How these distinct sources of representational variation affect low-data molecular generation has not been clearly studied. Here, using 1,000 seed molecules to train an autoregressive sequence model, we compare canonical SAFE with randomized SAFE at increasing corpus sizes, isolate atom-order and fragment-order axes of SAFE randomization, and compare fully randomized SAFE with randomized SMILES at molecule-by-molecule matched training corpora. Three findings emerge. First, randomization of SAFE alone raises the genuine yield of novel molecules more than 450-fold, turning a model that merely reproduces its training set into a practical molecular generator. Second, the two axes of randomization act jointly rather than additively: atom order alone reaches a tenth, and fragment order alone a seventh, of the genuine yield obtained when both vary, which is four times their combined contribution. Third, at matched corpus size and compute, randomized SAFE delivers 2.8 times the genuine yield of randomized SMILES. items.title: AtomSteer: Test-Time Constraint Steering for Atomistic Generative Models
items.abstract: Diffusion and flow matching models offer scalable approaches to generating crystalline materials, molecular conformers, and protein-ligand complexes. However, satisfying crystallographic symmetry, structural geometry, and accurate stereochemistry remains challenging. Satisfying these requirements calls for corrections that preserve the geometry already captured by the pretrained model. In this work, we propose AtomSteer, a test-time inference framework for steering pretrained atomistic generative models with structural constraints. During sampling, AtomSteer corrects intermediate structure predictions with bounded local projections, graph-rigid stereochemical transformations, and projections over periodic symmetries, accepting updates that improve constraint satisfaction while limiting changes to the rest of the structure. We demonstrate AtomSteer across three pretrained backbones, FlowMM, ET-Flow, and Boltz-2, spanning de novo crystal generation and crystal structure prediction, molecular conformer generation, and protein-ligand complex structure prediction. AtomSteer improves space-group distribution coverage in de novo crystal generation and improves target space-group recovery in crystal structure prediction. AtomSteer improves molecular validity and E/Z stereochemical accuracy while retaining conformer ensemble fidelity. items.title: A unified coarse-grained neural network potential for the dynamics of biomolecular complexes
items.abstract: The behavior of biomolecular complexes is governed by chemically specific interactions and often involves rare events that atomistic molecular dynamics struggle to capture within accessible timescales. Here we introduce AMARO v2.0, a coarse-grained neural network potential that retains all heavy atoms and treats solvent implicitly. Hydrogen-aware bead types and total-charge conditioning provide a shared representation for proteins, drug-like molecules, and their complexes, including ternary protein-protein-ligand systems. The model preserves folded proteins and captures key features of protein conformational free-energy landscapes. Across 262 complexes spanning 11 targets, the learned potential retains most ligand poses, although quaternary structure reorientation is observed for the HIF2A ternary complex. In targeted case studies, AMARO v2.0 distinguishes the two protonation states of trypsin-benzamidine and reaches the crystal binding pose in 3.3-fold more trajectories than all-atom molecular mechanics at a fixed estimated GPU-time budget. The same framework also recovers a reference binding pose in TYK2 and supports binding free-energy estimation for both trypsin-benzamidine and TYK2-EJM31, although the resulting values are more energetically favorable than the experimental references. items.title: EVA-Flow: Learning Shared Chemistry for Unified Environment-Aware Molecular Conformation Generation
items.abstract: Molecular 3D structures underpin simulations of thermodynamics, kinetics, crystallization, and nucleation, making their accurate prediction central to drug discovery and materials design. However, molecular geometry can change dramatically across environments. Existing models either ignore environmental effects or train separate models for each environment. We hypothesize that transfer learning across contexts is possible for conformer generation and that a general model will perform better when training data are limited, as in ligand binding and crystallization. We introduce EVA-Flow, a unified framework for environment-aware molecular conformation generation that learns shared chemical structure and adapts it through environment-conditioned generative modeling. Across vacuum, protein-ligand docking, solvation, and crystal packing, pretraining and cross-environment finetuning provide their largest gains in the three data-scarce settings. Evaluation against multiple reference conformations shows that EVA-Flow covers a broad range of solvation conformations. Analyses of molecules shared across environments support its ability to generate different conformations for the same molecule in different environments.
